title: Archaeology of the City: Urban Planning in Ancient Israel and Its Social Implications
author: Ze'ev Herzog
publisher: Tel Aviv University, Institute of Archaeology
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted monograph. Summaries in project's own words only.
summary: Urban-form study covering, among much else, the early Iron Age 'enclosed settlement' plan (dwellings ringing an open center, e.g. Beersheba VII) used as the comparative model for the Ziklag placeholder layout. Herzog's career specialty is city-gate typology (his PhD dissertation, later published in German as Das Stadttor in Israel und in den Nachbarländern, 1986, underlies this 1997 monograph's own urban-planning synthesis); the chronological gate typology consistently attributed to his work in later citing literature runs two-chamber gates as the prevalent form through the eleventh and early tenth centuries BCE, with four-chamber gates appearing only at the very end of that window and the monumental six-chamber 'Solomonic' type (Megiddo/Hazor/Gezer) emerging only in the mid-tenth century BCE and after. Queue #20b researcher pass (2026-08-12): checked specifically for this typology as a citable basis for claim-hebron-gate-form's modest two-chamber rendering (2 Samuel 3:27, hebron-gate) — found it, via multiple independent secondary sources describing Herzog's typology and citing this 1997 book by name as its source.
